I am Zakaryae. If you are reading this, you have stumbled into my local environment.

For years, my work existed entirely in the high-level realm—digital marketing, creative direction, and building brand identities from the ground up. I was shaping the facade, but eventually, I realized I wanted to build the infrastructure.

So I stripped away the abstractions. I am currently studying software engineering at 1337 in Morocco, trading brand strategy for low-level mechanics and first-principles problem solving.

This OS is my digital workspace. Welcome to the machine.

posts.title: libft_and_raw_memory.txt
posts.body:
A couple of weeks into rebuilding the C standard library from scratch for my libft project, and my perspective on computing has fundamentally shifted.

When you are forced to write your own memory allocation routines and string manipulation functions, the magic of high-level languages completely disappears. You realize everything is just bytes, pointers, and the brutal honesty of the compiler.

Implementing the singly linked list (t_list) functions was the real turning point. It forces you to visualize exactly where your data lives in memory and how pointers connect the dots.

There is a specific kind of beauty in low-level C programming. It is just you and the raw mechanics of the hardware.

cards.title: malloc(size)
cards.definition: malloc reserves size bytes on the heap and returns a pointer to the first byte, or NULL if it fails. The memory is NOT initialised.
cards.metaphor: Renting a storage unit. The pointer is the only key. Lose the key and the unit stays rented forever.
cards.recall: What does malloc return when it fails?
cards.recallAnswer: NULL. Always check it before using the pointer.

cards.title: free(ptr)
cards.definition: free releases a block obtained from malloc. Call it exactly once per malloc. Afterwards the pointer still holds the old address (it dangles) but the memory is no longer yours.
cards.metaphor: Handing the unit back. The key in your pocket still shows the old number, but the unit now belongs to someone else.
cards.visual:
[ ptr ] -x-> [ freed ]
 ptr = NULL;   (drop the stale key)
cards.recall: Why set the pointer to NULL after free?
cards.recallAnswer: free(NULL) is harmless, and an accidental use fails loudly instead of silently touching freed memory.

cards.title: Leaks
cards.definition: A leak is heap memory that is still allocated but no longer reachable through any pointer, so it can never be freed.
cards.metaphor: Dropping the only key into a river. The unit is still yours, and nobody can open it.
cards.visual:
s = malloc(8);   [ A ]
 s = malloc(16);  [ B ]   <- A has no pointer left
cards.recall: Which line makes the first block unreachable?
cards.recallAnswer: The second assignment. It overwrites the only pointer to the first block.

leak.prompt: Click the line that leaks memory.
leak.hint: Look for a block that is allocated but never used or freed.
leak.explain: tmp is allocated on line 7 and never freed or used. The block is lost the moment the function returns.

peer.q: What happens if malloc returns NULL and you dereference it?
peer.a: Undefined behaviour, usually a segfault. Check every malloc, and free what you already allocated before returning NULL.

peer.q: Stack versus heap: what is the difference?
peer.a: Stack memory is automatic and released when the function returns. Heap memory is managed manually with malloc/free and lives until you free it.

peer.q: How do you check a program for leaks?
peer.a: Run it under valgrind --leak-check=full. Blocks reported as definitely lost are leaks. Every malloc needs a matching free.

peer.q: Norminette: how long may a function be, and what else is limited?
peer.a: 25 lines (braces not counted), 5 variables, 4 parameters and 80 columns per line.

peer.q: Norminette: can you use for loops or ternaries?
peer.a: No. The Norm forbids for, do...while, switch, case, goto and ternary operators. Use while.

cards.title: A pointer is an address
cards.definition: A pointer stores the memory address of another value. *p reads the value at that address and &x gives the address of x.
cards.metaphor: A house number on an envelope. The pointer is the number, the house is the value.
cards.recallAnswer: 7. p points at x, so writing through p changes x.

cards.title: Pointer arithmetic
cards.definition: Adding n to a pointer moves it by n elements, not n bytes. p + 1 advances by sizeof(*p) bytes.
cards.metaphor: Walking down a street. +1 means "next house", however wide the houses are.
cards.visual:
int arr[3]
 [ a0 ][ a1 ][ a2 ]
   p    p+1   p+2
cards.recall: p is an int * at 0x1000 and sizeof(int) is 4. What is p + 3?

cards.title: void * and raw bytes
cards.definition: A void * holds an address with no type, so you cannot dereference it or do arithmetic on it. Cast to unsigned char * to walk byte by byte, as ft_memcpy does.
cards.metaphor: A sealed box with an address label but no description. You must say "treat it as bytes" before you open it.
cards.visual:
void *src --cast--> unsigned char *s
 [ b0 ][ b1 ][ b2 ] ...
cards.recall: Why cast a void * to unsigned char * in ft_memcpy?
cards.recallAnswer: To step one byte at a time. Arithmetic on void * is not standard C.

leak.prompt: Click the line that uses a dangling pointer.
leak.hint: Something is used after it has been given back.
leak.explain: Line 8 reads s after free(s). The pointer still holds the old address, but the memory is no longer yours: use-after-free.

peer.q: What does p + 1 do when p is an int *?
peer.a: It moves forward by sizeof(int) bytes, to the next int.

peer.q: What is the difference between *p++ and (*p)++?
peer.a: *p++ reads the value at p and then advances the pointer. (*p)++ increments the value being pointed at.

peer.q: Why can you not dereference a void *?
peer.a: The compiler does not know the size or type of the data it points to.

peer.q: Norminette: where do variables get declared?
peer.a: At the top of the function, one declaration per line, and declaration and assignment cannot share a line (except for constants and statics).

cards.title: A node
cards.definition: A t_list node holds a payload (void *content) and a pointer to the next node. The last node's next pointer is NULL.
cards.metaphor: Train carriages. Each one carries cargo and a hook to the next carriage. The last hook is empty.
cards.recall: What marks the end of the list?
cards.recallAnswer: A next pointer equal to NULL.

cards.title: ft_lstadd_front
cards.definition: Make the new node point at the old head, then make the new node the head. Order matters: link first, then move the head.
cards.metaphor: Couple the new carriage to the front of the train before announcing it is the new engine.
cards.visual:
new->next = *lst;   new -> [old head] -> ...
 *lst = new;        head = new
cards.recall: What breaks if you write *lst = new before new->next = *lst?
cards.recallAnswer: The old head is lost, new->next ends up pointing at new itself, and every old node leaks.

cards.title: ft_lstclear
cards.definition: Walk the list. Save next BEFORE freeing the node, call del on the content, free the node, and finally set *lst to NULL.
cards.metaphor: Scrapping a train. Note where the next hook leads before you scrap this carriage, or you will never find the rest.
cards.recall: Why store next before calling free?
cards.recallAnswer: After free the node memory is invalid. Reading node->next afterwards is a use-after-free.

leak.prompt: Click the line that causes the leak.
leak.hint: The node is freed, but what did it point to?
leak.explain: free(*lst) releases the node but never passes its content to del, so every payload leaks. Call del((*lst)->content) first.

peer.q: How do you find the last node of a list?
peer.a: Loop while node->next is not NULL. ft_lstlast returns that node, or NULL for an empty list.

peer.q: Why does ft_lstadd_back take a t_list **?
peer.a: The head may change when the list is empty, so the function needs the address of the head pointer.
Call del on the content, then free the node itself. It must not touch the following nodes.

peer.q: What should ft_lstmap do when an allocation fails?
peer.a: Clear the partially built new list with ft_lstclear and return NULL, so nothing leaks.
